newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK consumer credit to stay strong in June.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK consumer credit to stay strong in June.

text.p: British consumers continued to borrow heavily in June to fund the high street spending habit that is the main threat to Britain's low-inflation environment.
A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus forecast of a one billion stg increase in net consumer credit last month, a little down from May's 1.105 billion rise, but sturdy growth nonetheless.
The figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Tuesday and, as the key release in an otherwise quiet week, will be under the microscope of the financial markets.

Neil Parker, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, agreed with the consensus forecast and said the large rise in borrowing in May could have reflected consumer borrowing in advance of windfall payments from building societies.
Several of Britain's mutual lenders have converted into banks over the summer and handed out about 35 billion pounds in free shares to millions of members in the process.

Parker said consumer borrowing should now ease off. "We expect the growth of consumer credit will abate somewhat as consumers first use windfall payouts to pay for goods rather than use credit and then the increases in interest rates will have had time to take effect."
Base rates have been ratcheted up in three quarter-point moves, to 6.75 percent, in as many months as the Bank of England tries to take the heat out of the consumer boom.
Further increases are likely, and the next may come as early as next week when the Bank's monetary policy committee meets.

David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, noted figures released by the British Bankers' Association two weeks ago showed consumer lending by the major banks rose by 526 million stg in June, compared with a 595 million jump in May.
Net credit card lending was particularly weak, rising by just 126 million pounds over the month, the BBA said.

"This may suggest that some households are using the windfall gains to pay off outstanding debt, although there also seem to be many who are using them to finance current consumption," Philpotts said.
Economists are hoping the windfall effect will soon blow over, precisely because the payments are one-offs.

Retail sales figures, released last week, offered some solace in that direction. Within a 0.6 percent monthly increase in overall sales was a massive 7.5 percent leap in the sales of household goods -- consumer durables such as televisions, washing machines and stereos.
While that sort of spending could fuel inflation, it is not the sort of purchase that is repeated very quickly.
Earlier this month Clive Vaughan of retail consultant Verdict Research said he was relaxed about the windfall-fuelled spending spree.

He said consumers remain price sensitive and added "Windfall gains are very much a one-off. You would expect them to be hitting June and July sales in a big way, but there is no reason that should cause inflation. Retailers are not going to try and stick prices up for two months and then bring them down again." -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7708
